title: Sell Mineral Rights in Guernsey County, OH
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Guernsey County, OH
metaDescription: Own severed minerals under Cambridge, Byesville or Old Washington? Learn what Guernsey County's Utica Core position means for a sale and get a no-pressure offer.
heroLead: Guernsey County sits inside the Utica/Point Pleasant core fairway, and that single fact changes almost every question a mineral owner here needs answered before selling.
intro: Guernsey County runs along the I-70/I-77 interchange in east-central Ohio, with Cambridge as the county seat and Byesville, Old Washington, Quaker City and Senecaville rounding out the towns most owners recognize on a deed. Before the Utica/Point Pleasant play arrived, this county's economy leaned on coal and glass manufacturing, and a lot of the mineral fractions changing hands today trace back to farm deeds and coal-severance paperwork written decades before anyone drilled a horizontal well.

That coal-era paperwork matters. Older Guernsey County deeds frequently severed coal, oil and gas into separate estates, sometimes without naming every heir clearly, and those severed strings have been passed down, split among children, and occasionally forgotten. If you're holding a mineral interest here and wondering what it's worth or whether it's even still enforceable, the answer depends on the deed history, the county recorder's index, and whether the interest has stayed active under Ohio law.

sections.heading: Where Guernsey County sits in the Utica/Point Pleasant play
paragraphs: Guernsey County is generally regarded as part of the Utica/Point Pleasant core, the same structural trend running through Belmont, Harrison, Noble and Monroe counties to the east and south. Operators active in the broader core fairway over the life of the play have included names like Antero Resources, Gulfport Energy and XTO Energy, though which company holds a given lease can change hands through acquisition, so the operator listed on your last division order may not match who's actually running the well today.

Depth and pressure in the Point Pleasant here tend to support longer laterals than the shallower, older Clinton sandstone wells this county has hosted since long before Utica ever came up. If your deed only mentions 'oil and gas' with no formation named, both zones may be covered, which is one more reason a buyer needs the actual lease and any pooling or unitization order before pricing an interest.

sections.heading: The Ohio Dormant Mineral Act and why Guernsey County sees real disputes over it
paragraphs: Ohio Revised Code 5301.56, the Dormant Mineral Act, lets a surface owner reclaim a severed mineral interest that's gone unused for 20 straight years, no lease, no royalty payment, no title transaction, no separate tax listing, nothing on record showing the mineral owner still exists as far as the county is concerned. In coal counties like Guernsey, where minerals were severed generations ago and heirs scattered, this comes up constantly.

The mechanics matter more than people expect. The Ohio Supreme Court's 2016 decision in Corban v. Chesapeake Exploration settled that the older 1989 version of the statute never worked automatically. A surface owner has to follow the 2006 procedure: serve notice on the mineral holder (or publish notice if they can't be located), then record an affidavit of abandonment with the county recorder. The mineral owner then has 60 days to file a claim to preserve the interest or a lease, royalty record, or other savings event on record defeats the abandonment attempt entirely. Dodd v. Croskey, decided by the Seventh District in 2013, reinforced that filing a preservation claim inside that window is enough to keep the interest alive even without production. If you've received a DMA notice, or you suspect your family's mineral interest might be vulnerable to one, that's usually the moment to get real clarity on what you own before deciding whether to sell or defend it.

sections.heading: Checking what you actually own before you talk price
paragraphs: The Guernsey County Recorder's office in Cambridge holds the grantor/grantee index going back well over a century, and that's where a title search starts: tracing the severance deed, every subsequent conveyance of the mineral fraction, and any lease or division order that shows the interest was ever put to use. Heirship gets complicated fast when an original owner died without a will, or when a 1940s farm deed reserved '1/2 of all oil, gas and mineral rights' without specifying whether that's a full 50% or half of whatever fraction the grantor actually held.

A royalty statement, if you're receiving one, is the fastest way to confirm your net mineral acreage and decimal interest, since it shows the well's spacing unit and your share of it directly. If you've never received a statement and only have an old deed, expect any serious buyer to run a title search before making a firm offer, because an unclear chain of title is the single biggest thing that slows a closing down.

faqs.question: Is all of Guernsey County inside the Utica core, or does it vary by township?
faqs.answer: It varies. The county sits within the broader core fairway, but well results, lateral lengths and actual production differ township to township depending on depth to the Point Pleasant and where a spacing unit falls relative to the structural sweet spot. Two neighboring parcels can have very different histories depending on which unit they were pooled into.

faqs.question: I received a letter about abandoning my mineral rights under Ohio law. What do I do?
faqs.answer: Don't ignore it. Under the current Dormant Mineral Act procedure, you generally have 60 days from being served notice to file a claim to preserve your interest with the county recorder, or point to a lease, royalty payment or other savings event already on record. Missing that window is how families lose minerals they didn't know were at risk.

faqs.question: How do I find out if my Guernsey County mineral rights are still tied to an active lease?
faqs.answer: Start with the county recorder's index for any lease recorded against your parcel, then check whether that lease has been held by production, meaning a well on the pooled unit is still producing and paying royalties. An expired, undeveloped lease with no producing well behaves very differently in a sale than one actively held.

faqs.question: Do I need to sell my whole interest, or can I sell part of it?
faqs.answer: Most owners can sell all or a portion of their net mineral acres, and some choose to sell only the interest under one well or spacing unit while keeping the rest. What's possible depends on how your interest is described in the chain of title, so that's a question worth asking early in the conversation, not after an offer is already on the table.

faqs.question: What does 'severed mineral interest' actually mean for my Guernsey County property?
faqs.answer: It means the oil, gas and mineral rights under your land were separated from the surface at some point, often by a coal-era or farm-era deed, and now belong to whoever holds that reserved interest, which may or may not still be you or your family. Surface ownership and mineral ownership are two separate legal estates once a severance deed is recorded.
